Gold/Platinum Ratio

This ratio shows how many ounces of platinum are equivalent to one ounce of gold. Historically, platinum was more expensive than gold; when the ratio exceeds 1, gold is trading at a premium to platinum.

Loading Gold/Platinum Ratio data…

Why investors watch this ratio

A Gold/Platinum ratio above 1.0 means gold is more expensive than platinum — a historically unusual condition that some analysts consider a mean-reversion signal.

The ratio can reflect shifts in industrial demand (platinum has significant industrial uses in catalytic converters and hydrogen fuel cells) versus investment demand (gold is primarily held as a store of value).

When platinum was more expensive than gold

For most of the period between 1986 and 2008, platinum traded above gold — sometimes significantly so. At its peak in 2008, platinum briefly touched $2,300 per ounce while gold was around $1,000, giving a ratio of roughly 0.4 (meaning you needed less than half an ounce of platinum to buy one ounce of gold). That era reflected strong diesel autocatalyst demand in Europe and supply constraints from South African mines, which produce roughly 75% of the world's platinum.

Since 2011, the ratio has inverted and has not recovered. Gold's monetary premium has expanded enormously through successive crises — the European debt crisis, COVID-19, persistent inflation fears — while platinum has faced structural headwinds from declining European diesel vehicle sales and concerns about electric vehicle adoption reducing autocatalyst demand. In 2026, with gold near $3,500 per ounce and platinum roughly three times cheaper, the Gold/Platinum ratio sits around 3.0–3.3, close to its widest spread in the modern era.

The hydrogen economy thesis and what it means for the ratio

The new variable in the platinum story is hydrogen. Platinum is the preferred catalyst in proton-exchange membrane (PEM) fuel cells and green hydrogen electrolyzers. As governments in Europe, Japan, South Korea, China and the United States accelerate net-zero commitments, the World Platinum Investment Council has projected that hydrogen applications could become a material source of platinum demand by the early 2030s. This is a demand driver that palladium — often grouped with platinum as a platinum group metal — does not share. If the hydrogen buildout accelerates faster than current forecasts, the Gold/Platinum ratio could compress sharply from its current historically wide level.

The counter-thesis is that EV adoption removes autocatalyst demand faster than hydrogen creates new demand. Battery electric vehicles do not require catalytic converters of any kind. If BEV adoption runs faster than green hydrogen infrastructure is built, platinum loses its largest existing demand category before the new one fills the gap. The ratio's future direction depends heavily on which of these two trends wins.

How GoldAlert calculates this ratio

GoldAlert divides the daily closing price of gold (XAU/USD) by the daily closing price of platinum (XPT/USD) using the same calendar date for both. A ratio above 1.0 means gold costs more per ounce than platinum. A ratio of 3.0, for example, means one ounce of gold buys three ounces of platinum at current prices. The chart on this page shows how the ratio has moved over time, so you can see whether the current reading represents an unusually wide or narrow spread by historical standards.
